name: Olivine-Barrens
description: Olivine-Barrens wears its name in its skin: vast dust seas of pale green-gray mineral sweep from horizon to horizon, broken only by canyon systems that plunge six kilometers into dark, banded rock. The thin atmosphere does little more than stir the surface, raising slow amber-tinted dust storms that take weeks to cross a single basin. Sunlight falls hard and white through the near-vacuum, drawing sharp lines across terrain that has not changed in a million years.

The world feels abandoned rather than dead, like a house left mid-sentence. Wind through the canyon mouths produces low, mournful tones that carry for kilometers across the plains, the closest thing this planet has to a voice. Nights are bitter and star-thick; days are merely less cold, and the green dust gives everything underfoot the pallor of old bone.

Halfway down the largest canyon stands an abandoned mining complex, its ore loaders still parked in perfect row, its habitation modules sealed from the inside. The company that claimed the site dissolved before its first shipment ever lifted, and no record explains why the crews sealed the doors behind them or where they went afterward. Prospectors who have cut the seals report personal effects neatly stowed, meals half-eaten, and platinum ore still sitting in the hoppers.

The ore is real, and rich, which is precisely the problem: every claim-jumper who descends into the canyon spends a night in those silent modules first, and more than one has come back up refusing to say what they heard in the wind. Independent surveyors now sell maps with the complex marked as a hazard rather than a prize. The platinum remains in its hoppers, the doors remain sealed, and the canyons keep singing over all of it.
